cls.function: Amendatory bill: adds section 3119 to title 18 and section 1979A to the Revised Statutes
cls.banner: If enacted, this would change existing law. It would require a warrant for government searches, including access to data held by companies, and let people sue federal officials for Fourth Amendment violations.
cls.checks: All families run. For an amendatory bill, fit with the surrounding statutes, definitions and remedies come first.
purpose.ladder.mechanism: Require a warrant before the government searches or accesses third-party data, and create a lawsuit against federal officials.
purpose.ladder.outcome: Government agencies stop obtaining Americans' personal data without a judge's approval.
purpose.ladder.aim: An end to warrantless mass surveillance.
promises.0.p: A universal warrant requirement for government searches
promises.0.why: The rule is stated broadly, but "the government" is never defined, "search" is tied to a court-made test, several definitions reach only searches aimed at a "specific" person, and the bill does not say how it relates to existing surveillance statutes.
promises.1.p: Federal and local agencies both covered
promises.1.why: The text says "the government" and "a government entity" without saying whether that includes States and localities. The lawsuit provision reaches only people acting under federal law.
promises.2.why: A direct ban on warrantless access to third-party data is in the text. It sits beside an undefined consent exception, a public-information exception and a definition of "search" built on the test that produced the doctrine.
promises.3.p: Ban on federal purchase of commercially available location data
promises.3.why: The text bars "access" to data held by data brokers without a warrant, which would cover purchases. It does not mention purchase, sale or contractors, and places no duty on the seller.
promises.4.p: No warrantless facial recognition or license plate tracking tied to individuals
promises.4.why: Subsection (c) is written as a limit on the exceptions, not as a prohibition, and its syntax leaves its reach open to more than one reading.
promises.5.p: Prohibit federal pressure on local law enforcement to share warrantlessly collected data
promises.5.why: No provision of the introduced text addresses data sharing between federal and local agencies or conditions on federal grants.
promises.6.p: People whose rights are violated can sue for damages
promises.6.why: The lawsuit covers rights "secured by the Fourth Amendment", not the new warrant rule in section 3119, and the text is silent on the immunity defenses courts apply to the statute it copies.
questions.0.q: The long title promises warrants for searches that "significantly impinge on the privacy or security of a person". Where does that standard appear in the operative text?
questions.0.a: It does not. The operative definition of "search" uses a different test, a "reasonable expectation of privacy". A court comparing title to text would give effect to the text.
questions.1.q: Who is "the government" in "The government shall not access"?
questions.1.a: The bill does not say. The new section sits in the federal criminal procedure title, and the lawsuit provision is limited to people acting under color of federal law. One sponsor's release says local agencies are covered. If States are meant to be bound, the bill needs to say so and rest on a constitutional power that allows it.
questions.2.q: Who creates, holds, moves, sells and uses the data this bill is about, and where on that chain does the bill act?
questions.2.a: Apps, carriers, banks and device makers collect it. Data brokers aggregate and sell it. Agencies and their contractors buy or demand it. The bill acts at one point only: the government's access. It places no duty on the companies that collect or sell.
questions.3.q: Who has obtained this kind of data without a warrant before, and on what theory?
questions.3.a: After the Supreme Court required a warrant for cell-site location records in 2018, a Defense Intelligence Agency memo disclosed in 2021 said the agency bought commercial smartphone location data and did not read the ruling to require a warrant for purchased data. A declassified 2022 report to the Director of National Intelligence described large-scale purchases of commercially available information across the intelligence community.
questions.4.q: If direct access without a warrant is closed, what is the next cheapest path to the same information?
questions.4.a: The text leaves several. Rely on an existing statute that authorizes collection on a lower standard and argue this general rule did not repeal it. Collect in bulk, since two definitions reach only searches of a "specific" person. Query data already held, since the data definition speaks of "acquisition and analysis" together. Rely on someone's "consent". Treat purchased data as publicly available. Have a contractor or partner agency hold the data.
questions.5.q: Which existing laws let agencies obtain third-party data on less than a probable-cause warrant, and what does the bill say about them?
questions.5.a: Several do, including court orders and subpoenas under the Stored Communications Act, national security letters, foreign intelligence collection under section 702 of FISA, and mandatory financial reporting. The bill mentions none of them and has no clause saying it overrides other law. Courts disfavor implied repeals and generally let a specific statute govern over a general one.
questions.6.q: If an agency searches without a warrant in violation of new section 3119, what happens?
questions.6.a: Section 3119 has no remedy of its own. Evidence is not excluded, since no suppression rule is provided. The new lawsuit covers Fourth Amendment violations, which may not include conduct that only the statute forbids. An official sued under it can be expected to raise the immunity defenses courts apply to the parallel civil rights statute.
questions.7.q: Exception (5) allows "searches conducted with consent". Whose consent?
questions.7.a: The text does not say. Paragraph (a)(2)(A) says a third party's consent cannot substitute for a warrant, and (a)(2)(B) limits waiver by contract, but the exception itself is unqualified.
questions.8.q: Who bears the effects if this works exactly as written?
questions.8.a: People whose data is held by companies gain a warrant rule against the government. The same data would still be collected, sold to private buyers and exposed to breach. Investigators lose tools they use lawfully today, including in fraud, child exploitation and missing-person cases, which is the trade-off critics raise.
questions.9.q: Does anyone have to report, audit or count what happens under this bill?
questions.9.a: No. There is no reporting requirement, inspector general role or audit, so Congress and the public would have no routine way to learn whether warrantless access had stopped.
questions.10.q: What is the smallest set of changes that would make the text match what is promised?
questions.10.a: Define "government". Make the lawsuit cover violations of section 3119. Say how the section relates to existing surveillance statutes. Specify whose consent counts. Reach bulk collection and data already held. Add a suppression rule. The broader aim of ending the trade in this data would need a separate provision aimed at sellers.
findings.S1.title: The warrant requirement applies to "the government", a term the bill does not define.
findings.S1.plain: The bill says "the government" may not access your data without a warrant and never says which governments. That openness could be a strength, reaching every agency at every level, or a gap, if it is read to mean federal law enforcement only.
findings.S1.tech: Section 3119 uses "the government", "government-initiated" and "a government entity or its agents" without definition. Chapter 205 of title 18 governs federal criminal procedure, and new section 1979A reaches only action under color of federal law, both of which point toward a federal-only reading. One sponsor's release says local agencies are covered. If States are covered, a statutory rule broader than the Fourth Amendment as courts read it would need a constitutional basis for binding them, which invites challenge.
findings.S1.use: A state or local agency argues the section does not apply to it. A federal agency obtains the same data from a state or local partner.
findings.S1.am.S1b.label: Keep it open, but name the hard cases
findings.S1.am.S1b.cost: Uses "includes", which the House and Senate drafting manuals reserve for a definition that is not exhaustive, so the term stays open while the three documented gaps are named. Naming States outright raises the federalism question, which the narrower option avoids.
findings.S1.am.S1a.label: Define it as a closed list
findings.S1.am.S1a.cost: A closed definition gives certainty and loses the breadth of the open term: anything not listed is presumed excluded. This version also reaches States only through federal involvement.
findings.S1.inq.q: Which real actors fall on each side of the line depending on what "the government" means?
findings.S1.inq.items.0.h: State police running searches for a federal agency
findings.S1.inq.items.0.d: Audit logs show Florida's wildlife police ran license plate lookups for Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with each search querying more than 5,000 camera networks. The federal agency had no contract with the camera company. If "the government" means federal agencies only, the state officer's search is outside the rule.
findings.S1.inq.items.1.h: Federal searches of locally collected data
findings.S1.inq.items.1.d: University of Washington researchers found Border Patrol ran hundreds if not thousands of searches of local police plate data through a nationwide lookup setting. California's attorney general wrote to 20 police departments about federal access and sued one.
findings.S1.inq.items.2.d: The disclosed purchases of location data were made by the Defense Intelligence Agency. The new section sits in the criminal procedure title of the U.S. Code, which governs law enforcement. The text does not say that defense and intelligence components are "the government" for this purpose.
findings.S1.inq.items.3.h: The lawsuit is narrower than the rule
findings.S1.inq.items.3.d: Section 1979A reaches only persons acting under color of federal law. A state officer who runs a search for a federal agency could be sued, if at all, only under the existing civil rights statute and only for a constitutional violation.
findings.S1.inq.open: No court has read this language. The sponsors' releases disagree with each other on whether local agencies are covered.
findings.S1.two.dec: Which entity construes "the government" in the first instance, given that the bill names no implementing agency and the cause of action reaches only federal actors?
findings.S1.two.views.0.why: One sponsor's release says local agencies are covered, which the text does not say.
findings.S2.title: The bill defines "search" by the reasonable-expectation-of-privacy test, from which the third-party doctrine derives.
findings.S2.plain: The bill defines a search as something that intrudes on a "reasonable expectation of privacy". Courts used that same phrase to decide that people have no such expectation in data they share with companies. The bill's title uses yet another standard, searches that "significantly impinge" on privacy, which appears nowhere in the operative text.
findings.S2.tech: The third-party doctrine holds that a person has no reasonable expectation of privacy in information voluntarily conveyed to a third party; the Supreme Court narrowed it for cell-site location records in 2018 without overruling it. The definition then lists items (A) through (C) after "including the following". It is unclear whether the listed items are searches regardless of the expectation test or only examples that must still satisfy it. Paragraph (a)(2) is drafted as a separate command and does not depend on the definition, which helps. The long title's phrase "significantly impinge on the privacy or security of a person" is a third formulation. Courts may consult a title to resolve ambiguity in the text, so the title gives a party arguing for a narrow reading one more thing to cite.
findings.S2.use: A defendant agency argues that access to shared data is not a "search" under subsection (d) because no reasonable expectation of privacy exists, points to the title to say only significant intrusions were meant, and argues paragraph (a)(2) is limited the same way.
findings.S2.am.S2a.label: Make the list independent of the test
findings.S2.am.S2a.cost: A definition this broad, read with subparagraph (C), makes nearly any government handling of personal information a search. That increases the pressure for clear exceptions.
findings.S3.title: Two of the three definitions of "search" are limited to acts directed at a specific person.
findings.S3.plain: Two of the three definitions of a search cover acts aimed at a "specific" person. Collecting data on everyone at once is, by its nature, not aimed at anyone specific.
findings.S3.tech: Subparagraph (A) covers acts "purposefully directed at a specific person or entity". Subparagraph (B) covers surveillance that "collects information on a specific individual or entity". Only subparagraph (C) lacks the qualifier, and it has its own limit (see the next finding). Bulk or dragnet collection is the practice the sponsors describe as the problem.
findings.S3.use: An agency characterizes a program as untargeted bulk acquisition, outside (A) and (B).
findings.S3.am.S3a.label: Add bulk collection by name
findings.S3.am.S3a.cost: A warrant must particularly describe what is sought, so bulk acquisition would in practice be barred, not just regulated. That is a policy decision with consequences for agencies that analyze aggregate data for non-investigative purposes.
findings.S4.title: The phrase "acquisition and analysis" is conjunctive and may be read to require both acts.
findings.S4.plain: The data definition covers the "acquisition and analysis" of personal data. Read strictly, an agency that searches data it already holds is analyzing without acquiring.
findings.S4.tech: "And" is ordinarily conjunctive. Subsection (c) separately lists "collection, retention, querying, or analysis", which shows the drafters knew how to list the acts disjunctively. Queries of previously collected data are a central issue in the current surveillance debate.
findings.S4.use: Data acquired before enactment, or acquired lawfully under another authority, is queried later without a warrant.
findings.S4.am.S4a.label: List the acts separately
findings.S4.am.S4a.cost: Making retention itself a search needs a transition rule for data agencies hold today.
findings.S5.title: The consent exception does not specify whose consent is required.
findings.S5.plain: Searches "with consent" need no warrant. The bill does not say whose consent counts: the person the data is about, or the company holding it.
findings.S5.tech: Paragraph (a)(2)(A) bars access to third-party data "regardless of whether the third party consents", and (a)(2)(B) restricts waiver by contract unless "knowing, voluntary, and explicit". But subsection (b) is introduced by "The following may be conducted without a warrant" and paragraph (5) is unqualified. Only (a)(1) is expressly made subject to subsection (b), so how (b)(5) interacts with (a)(2) is left to inference.
findings.S5.use: A click-through that is labeled knowing, voluntary and explicit satisfies (a)(2)(B), and consent under (b)(5) is then claimed for everything that follows.
findings.S5.am.S5a.label: Specify the consenting person
findings.S5.am.S5a.cost: Third-party consent has legitimate uses, such as a business reporting a crime against itself using its own records. A carve-out for a third party's own business records about its own victimization may be needed.
findings.S6.title: The public-information exception does not require that the subject of the information be the person who made it public.
findings.S6.plain: Information "made available by a person or entity to a public audience" needs no warrant. The text does not require that the person the information is about be the one who made it public.
findings.S6.tech: Paragraph (b)(3) turns on publication "by a person or entity", any person or entity. Agencies have described purchased datasets as commercially or publicly available. Subsection (c) limits the exceptions for data "exposed to public view or accessible to a third party", but only "with respect to data gathered by entering a public place" and similar settings.
findings.S6.use: A dataset offered for sale to any buyer is treated as made available to a public audience.
findings.S6.am.S6a.label: Tie publication to the individual
findings.S6.am.S6a.cost: Narrowing this far could require a warrant to read a news article about someone. Paragraph (4), which covers news outlets and public records, would carry that load and should be checked alongside.
findings.S8.title: The provision on facial recognition and license plate readers is syntactically ambiguous and may be read narrowly.
findings.S8.plain: The sentence meant to protect people from face scanning and license plate tracking is a single long clause with several conditions. It can be read to cover much less than the sponsors describe.
findings.S8.tech: Subsection (c) is a rule of construction for the exceptions, not a prohibition. It applies "if the person associated with the collected identifiers did not express informed and voluntary consent to such collection with respect to data gathered by entering a public place, operating a motor vehicle on a public roadway, or patronizing a private establishment open to the public". The trailing "with respect to" phrase can modify the consent or the whole rule. The two listed data types follow "including", leaving open whether other data is covered.
findings.S8.use: Data gathered in a setting not listed, such as an online platform, is argued to be outside the limitation.
findings.S8.am.S8a.label: Restate as a direct prohibition
findings.S8.am.S8a.cost: A flat rule would reach ordinary uses such as checking a plate during a traffic stop. Exception (2) covers identity documents but not plates, so the stop-and-check case needs its own treatment.
findings.S9.title: The savings clause for "ordinary" law enforcement encounters does not define the term.
findings.S9.plain: The bill says nothing in it restricts searches "incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters". It does not say what makes an encounter ordinary.
findings.S9.tech: Paragraph (e)(3) preserves authority to conduct detentions, frisks, arrests "or searches incident to ordinary criminal law enforcement encounters". The familiar doctrine is search incident to arrest. "Incident to ... encounters" is broader and undefined, and a rule of construction that preserves existing authority can be argued to override the new warrant rule wherever the two meet.
findings.S9.use: A device search during a routine stop is defended as incident to an ordinary encounter.
findings.S9.am.S9a.label: Use the recognized doctrine
findings.S9.am.S9a.cost: Narrower than current practice in some settings; law enforcement groups would object.
findings.S10.title: The cause of action covers constitutional violations and does not extend to the bill's statutory warrant requirement.
findings.S10.plain: The bill creates a new warrant rule in one section and a right to sue in another. The right to sue covers violations of the Fourth Amendment, not violations of the new rule. Where the new rule goes further than courts say the Constitution does, there may be nothing to sue over.
findings.S10.tech: Section 1979A creates liability for deprivation of rights "secured by the Fourth Amendment". Section 3119 is a statute. Its purpose is to require warrants in situations, such as third-party data, where current doctrine says the Fourth Amendment does not. A violation of 3119 that is not also a constitutional violation falls outside 1979A, and 3119 has no remedy clause of its own.
findings.S10.use: An agency concedes a statutory violation and wins dismissal because no constitutional right was infringed.
findings.S10.am.S10a.label: Add the statute to the cause of action
findings.S10.am.S10a.cost: Expands personal liability for federal employees to a new and untested statutory standard. Expect pressure to add a good-faith defense, which is the next finding.
findings.S10.inq.q: Which of the practices the bill targets would violate the new rule but not the Fourth Amendment as courts now read it?
findings.S10.inq.items.0.d: The Supreme Court held in 1976 that a customer has no Fourth Amendment interest in records held by a bank. The 2018 Carpenter decision said it did not disturb that rule. Warrantless access to bank records would breach new section 3119 and still not be a deprivation of a right "secured by the Fourth Amendment".
findings.S10.inq.items.1.d: The same is true of numbers dialed and similar records under the 1979 decision Carpenter also left in place.
findings.S10.inq.items.2.d: The Supreme Court has not ruled on purchased data. At least one agency has taken the position that the 2018 ruling does not require a warrant for it.
findings.S10.inq.items.3.h: Facial recognition and plate readers in public
findings.S10.inq.items.3.d: The Supreme Court has not held that either is a search. Subsection (c) of the bill tries to protect against both, and the lawsuit would not follow.
findings.S10.inq.open: Lower courts differ on some of these practices. The point holds wherever a court finds no constitutional search.
findings.S12.title: The attorney's fees provision refers to "this Act" in text that would be inserted into existing law.
findings.S12.plain: The attorney's fees clause refers to suits "to enforce this Act". The clause is being inserted into an old compilation of laws, where "this Act" has no clear meaning.
findings.S12.tech: Section 1979A(b) is new text of the Revised Statutes. Inside inserted text, "this Act" would ordinarily be read as the statute being amended, not the Surveillance Accountability Act. The parallel fee provision for civil rights suits refers to the sections by number.
findings.S12.use: A fee award is contested on the ground that the suit enforces a section, not an Act.
findings.S12.am.S12a.label: Refer to the section
findings.S13.title: The introduced text contains four drafting errors.
findings.S13.plain: The text misspells "Definitions", says "Searched conducted" where it means "Searches conducted", says "new outlets" where it means "news outlets", and leaves the word "is" out of an amending instruction.
findings.S13.tech: Three are harmless. "New outlets" in an exception could be argued to mean something other than news organizations. The clerical amendment "United States Code, amended by adding" lacks an operative verb.
findings.S13.use: Minimal, but errors in an exception clause are the kind that get litigated.
findings.S13.am.S13a.label: Correct all four
findings.S15.title: The third-party data prohibition, read literally, extends to routine regulatory reporting.
findings.S15.plain: The ban covers "any data" held by a third party. Read literally, that includes records agencies collect every day outside of surveillance, such as reports that banks and employers are required to file.
findings.S15.tech: Paragraph (a)(2)(A) is not limited to data about individuals, to investigations, or to compelled or purchased access. Mandatory reporting schemes, regulatory inspections and civil subpoenas all involve the government accessing data held by third parties. Courts faced with a rule this broad and no override clause tend to read it narrowly to avoid upending other statutes, and the narrowing can cut into the intended coverage.
findings.S15.use: The breadth becomes the argument for a narrow reading across the board.
findings.S15.am.S15a.label: Aim the rule at personal data sought for investigation or intelligence
findings.S15.am.S15a.cost: A purpose limit creates its own gap: data gathered for an administrative purpose can later be shared with investigators. A use restriction would be needed alongside.
findings.S7.title: The exigent-circumstances exception is undefined and carries no requirement of after-the-fact review.
findings.S7.plain: Emergencies are exempt from the warrant rule. The bill does not define an emergency or require anyone to review the claim afterward.
findings.S7.tech: Leaving the term undefined imports existing doctrine, which is a reasonable drafting choice. Other surveillance statutes that allow emergency access pair it with after-the-fact court approval within a fixed time.
findings.S7.use: Emergency access becomes routine where no one reviews it.
findings.S11.title: The cause of action does not address whether qualified immunity applies.
findings.S11.plain: The new right to sue copies the wording of the main civil rights statute. Courts let officials sued under that statute avoid damages unless the right was already clearly established. The bill does not say whether the same defense applies here.
findings.S11.tech: Section 1979A(a) tracks section 1979 of the Revised Statutes (42 U.S.C. 1983). Qualified immunity under that statute is a judicial doctrine, and a court would likely carry it over to parallel text absent a contrary instruction. For new surveillance technologies, the law is rarely clearly established. The Supreme Court has also sharply limited court-created damages suits against federal officers, which is why a statutory action matters and why its details do.
findings.S11.use: Damages claims fail at the outset on immunity grounds even where a violation occurred.
findings.S11.am.S11a.label: Address the defense and set minimum damages
findings.S11.am.S11a.cost: Removing immunity for federal employees is contested and would draw opposition from law enforcement and national security agencies. An alternative is to make the United States, not the individual, the liable party.
findings.S16.title: The bill contains no exclusionary rule for evidence obtained in violation of the warrant requirement.
findings.S16.plain: The bill does not say that evidence obtained without a required warrant must be kept out of court. Without that, the main everyday check on unlawful searches is missing for anything the bill adds beyond the Constitution.
findings.S16.tech: Suppression is a constitutional remedy. For purely statutory violations, courts generally do not exclude evidence unless the statute says so, as the federal wiretap law does.
findings.S16.use: Data obtained in violation of section 3119 is used in prosecutions and other proceedings.
findings.S16.am.S16a.label: Add an exclusion rule
findings.S16.am.S16a.cost: Exclusion can end prosecutions over drafting ambiguities elsewhere in the bill, which raises the stakes on every other finding.
findings.S17.title: The bill does not state how it interacts with existing statutes that authorize collection without a probable-cause warrant.
findings.S17.plain: Several laws already let agencies get data without a probable-cause warrant, including foreign intelligence law. This bill does not mention them or say that it wins if they conflict.
findings.S17.tech: There is no statement of how the section relates to other law and no conforming amendment to the Stored Communications Act, the national security letter statutes, the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act or financial reporting laws. Implied repeals are disfavored, and a specific statute ordinarily controls over a general one. Paragraph (e)(1) says the section does not "authorize surveillance that would otherwise be unlawful" but is silent on surveillance that is otherwise lawful. The Senate drafting manual advises against a general "notwithstanding any other provision of law" clause, on the ground that it is unlikely to have effect, and tells drafters to identify and cite the conflicting law.
findings.S17.use: An agency continues to use a specific existing authority and argues the general warrant rule left it intact. This is the most direct route around the bill for intelligence agencies.
findings.S17.am.S17a.label: Name the laws it overrides
findings.S17.am.S17a.cost: Cites each affected law by name, as the Senate drafting manual advises, in place of a general override. Anything not named survives, so the list has to be complete: financial reporting law and administrative subpoenas are left out here and would continue. It would restructure intelligence collection that touches Americans and move the bill to additional committees.
findings.S17.inq.q: Which specific existing authorities let agencies obtain covered data on less than a probable-cause warrant?
findings.S17.inq.items.0.d: Nearly 250,000 targets in 2022, approved by annual court certification and not by individual warrants. The FBI ran roughly 119,000 searches of the collected data using Americans' identifiers that year.
findings.S17.inq.items.1.h: Court orders under the Stored Communications Act
findings.S17.inq.items.1.d: 18 U.S.C. 2703(d) lets a court order disclosure of records on "specific and articulable facts", a lower standard than probable cause.
findings.S17.inq.items.2.d: 18 U.S.C. 2709 lets the FBI demand subscriber and transaction records on its own certification, with no judge.
findings.S17.inq.items.3.d: 31 U.S.C. 5318(g) requires banks to file suspicious activity reports with Treasury. The government receives financial data about named individuals with no warrant and no request.
findings.S17.inq.items.4.d: Dozens of statutes let agencies subpoena business records without a court, for example 21 U.S.C. 876 for drug investigations.
findings.S17.inq.items.5.d: Intelligence collection abroad proceeds under presidential authority, not statute. A general amendment to title 18 does not mention it.
findings.S17.inq.open: Statute citations are given so they can be checked; the sections themselves were not opened in this pass. The 2022 figures are the most recent that were verified.
findings.S17.two.dec: Is the bill intended to alter intelligence collection or only law enforcement practice?
findings.S17.two.views.0.why: Favor renewing current law and taking up reform afterward.
findings.S17.two.views.1.why: A coalition of groups has asked for a warrant rule on queries of intelligence data and for the broker loophole to be closed.
findings.S17.two.views.2.why: The lead sponsor has said there should be no reauthorization without a warrant requirement.
findings.S22.title: Under the Surveillance Accountability Act, each agency would decide whether its own data collection requires a warrant under section 3119, with no independent review when it decides that none is required.
findings.S22.plain: Section 3119, as the Surveillance Accountability Act would add it, requires a warrant from a neutral magistrate for a search. The agency that wants the data would decide in the first instance whether its conduct is a search and whether an exception for consent, public information or exigent circumstances applies. A judge would review the matter only if the agency concluded that a warrant was needed. The bill requires no report, audit or notice covering the cases in which the agency concluded that it was not.
findings.S22.tech: The warrant requirement supplies an independent check for searches that reach a court. The decisions that determine whether a matter reaches a court are left to the investigating agency, which benefits from a narrow reading of "search" and a broad reading of the exceptions in section 3119(b). The cause of action in section 1979A depends on the person searched learning of the search, and the bill has no notice requirement.
findings.S22.use: An agency could classify a data acquisition as outside section 3119, or as within the consent or exigent circumstances exception, and no court, inspector general or member of the public would be told of that decision.
findings.S22.am.S22a.label: Yearly audit of decisions not to seek a warrant
findings.S22.am.S22a.cost: A yearly audit by each agency's Inspector General would add cost, and a public summary would have to be written so that it does not expose investigative methods. Inspectors general are appointed within the executive branch, so an audit is less independent than review by a court.
findings.S18.title: The bill specifies no effective date and no rule for data already in agency possession.
findings.S18.plain: The bill does not say when it takes effect or what happens to data agencies already have.
findings.S18.tech: Without an effective date, the Act takes effect on enactment. There is no provision on retention, deletion or continued querying of data acquired earlier, and no treatment of pending investigations.
findings.S19.title: The bill imposes no reporting, audit or inspector general requirement.
findings.S19.plain: The bill has no reporting requirement, audit or inspector general role. There would be no regular way to know whether agencies had stopped.
findings.S19.tech: Surveillance statutes commonly require annual reports of orders sought and granted and periodic inspector general review. The lawsuit depends on people learning they were searched, and the bill has no notice requirement.
findings.S19.use: Violations that are never disclosed are never challenged.
findings.S21.title: A provision described in a sponsor's announcement, on federal pressure to share locally collected data, does not appear in the introduced text.
findings.S21.plain: One sponsor's announcement says the bill would stop federal agencies from pressuring local police to share surveillance data. No such provision appears in the introduced text.
findings.S21.tech: The release lists a prohibition on federal pressure on local law enforcement to share warrantlessly collected data. The text contains no provision on intergovernmental sharing, grant conditions or fusion centers. The provision may have been in an earlier draft.
findings.S21.use: Readers relying on the announcement believe the practice is addressed.
findings.S20.title: The bill restricts government acquisition from data brokers and does not regulate the collection or sale of the data.
findings.S20.plain: The bill tells the government not to access brokered data without a warrant. It does not stop companies from collecting that data or selling it. The data would still exist, and any gap in the government-side rule leads back to it.
findings.S20.tech: Disclosed practice shows why this matters: a 2021 Defense Intelligence Agency memo described purchases of commercial location data, and a declassified 2022 report described intelligence community purchases of commercially available information at scale. Supply-side designs exist. Montana in 2025 barred its own agencies from buying such data, and the House in 2024 passed a bill aimed at government purchases from brokers. None of these ends the collection itself.
findings.S20.use: Any agency or partner outside the bill's reach can still buy.
findings.S20.am.S20a.label: Option for the broader aim: act on the seller
findings.S20.am.S20a.cost: This goes beyond the bill's stated purpose. Restrictions on selling information face First Amendment challenges, "data broker" would need a definition, and companies that collect data directly are not brokers. Prohibiting the brokerage business altogether is a further step with larger economic effects and the same gap for first-party collectors.
findings.S20.two.dec: Is the objective to constrain government acquisition or to end the commercial trade in the data?
findings.S20.two.views.0.why: At least one agency has taken the view that purchased data needs no warrant.
bigger.issue: Fourth Amendment protection in the digital age
bigger.lead: Even if every provision worked as intended, this bill would put a warrant requirement on government access. It would not, by itself, end warrantless surveillance, for the reasons below.
bigger.map.0.part: Government access to data held by companies
bigger.map.1.note: Covered as "access"; purchase and contractors are not named.
bigger.map.2.part: Collection and sale of personal data by private companies
bigger.map.2.note: No duty on collectors or sellers. The data remains available to other buyers, including foreign ones.
bigger.map.3.part: Foreign intelligence collection that sweeps in Americans
bigger.map.3.note: Governed by separate statutes and executive authority the bill does not mention.
bigger.map.4.part: Existing lower-standard orders, subpoenas and national security letters
bigger.map.4.note: No override clause or conforming amendments.
bigger.map.5.note: Depends on the undefined term "the government".
bigger.map.6.part: Government-run sensors: facial recognition and plate readers
bigger.map.6.note: Addressed through a limit on exceptions with uncertain reach.
bigger.map.7.note: No retention, deletion or query rule for existing datasets.
bigger.map.8.part: Remedies when the rule is broken
bigger.map.8.note: A lawsuit for constitutional violations; no suppression rule; immunity not addressed.
bigger.map.9.note: No reporting, audit or notice to people searched.
stake.priv.want: A warrant rule with no gaps, and an end to government purchases from data brokers.
stake.fle.want: Fast lawful access to records in fraud, trafficking and missing-person cases. Critics of the bill say warrant requirements slow investigations.
stake.ic.want: Existing foreign intelligence authorities left intact.
stake.slp.want: Continued use of plate readers and shared databases, and a clear answer on whether the rule binds them.
stake.brok.role: Data brokers and advertising technology firms
stake.brok.want: To keep selling data, with government as one customer among many.
stake.hold.want: A clear rule on when they must hand data over, and no liability for following it.
stake.surv.want: Protection that does not depend on which agency is looking. Reporting shows local camera data reaching immigration enforcement.
stake.vict.want: Investigations that are not slowed when someone is in danger.
stake.spon.want: A warrant for every government search, described as covering federal and local agencies.
stake.opp.role: Members who favor renewing existing surveillance law first
stake.opp.want: Reauthorization of current authorities, with wider reform left for later.
stake.pl.role: Civil rights lawyers who would bring suits
stake.pl.want: A cause of action that survives a motion to dismiss.
stake.def.role: Government lawyers who would defend them
stake.def.want: The narrowest defensible reading of each duty.
stake.tex.role: A judge who reads statutes by their text
stake.tex.want: Applies the words as written and will not supply what Congress left out.
stake.pur.role: A judge who reads statutes by their purpose
stake.pur.want: Resolves doubt in favor of what the law was trying to do.
stake.olc.want: Wants every key term defined, every reference checked and every relationship to existing law stated.
conflicts.0.claim: Under the Surveillance Accountability Act, the agency that wants a person's data would decide whether its own collection of that data requires a warrant.
conflicts.0.detail: Each agency would decide whether its own acquisition of data is a search under section 3119 and whether an exception applies. A judge would review a search only when the agency concluded that a warrant was needed and applied for one. The bill requires no report or audit of the cases in which the agency concluded that no warrant was needed.
conflicts.1.who: Each agency that conducts a search
conflicts.1.claim: Under the Surveillance Accountability Act, the agency conducting a search would decide whether an emergency or consent excuses that search from the warrant requirement.
conflicts.1.detail: Exigent circumstances and consent are two of the exceptions in section 3119(b). The agency that benefits from an exception would decide whether it applies, and the bill requires no review after the agency relies on one.
conf_note: No conflicts involving named individuals have been researched for this bill, which is not law and assigns no duty to a named official.
